query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the nozzle-to-substrate distance to approximately 300 mm in the HVAF-i7 torch will boost particle velocity and kinetic energy, thereby enhancing deposition efficiency and producing a thicker, more adherent FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy bond coat with minimal in-spray oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder feedstock with a 15–45 μm size distribution, as previously optimized using the HVAF-M3 torch.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 processing parameters by setting the spray (nozzle-to-substrate) distance to around 300 mm, thereby increasing the in-flight particle velocity.
generation.conditions: Deposition is conducted under standard HVAF-i7 conditions optimized for minimal oxidation, on substrates including those with internal diameters as small as 120 mm, and under service conditions typical of high-temperature thermal-barrier applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic energy leads to more effective particle flattening and inter-splat bonding, resulting in reduced rebound losses and improved layer build-up, while maintaining a low oxidation level.
generation.mechanism: By increasing the spray distance, the particles gain additional acceleration resulting in higher impact energy at the substrate. This improved kinetic energy enhances melting and deformation upon impact, which increases deposition efficiency and coating thickness without significantly increasing as-sprayed oxidation due to the relatively shorter residence time in the oxygen-rich zone.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coating thickness is expected to improve significantly over the baseline (e.g., an increase of 20% or more), while retaining good adhesion and low in-spray oxidation comparable to that achieved with the optimal 15–45 μm feedstock in the HVAF-M3 system.
generation.baseline: FeCoNiCrAl bond coats deposited using 15–45 μm feedstock with the standard HVAF-i7 settings that yield acceptable quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: The optimized spray distance should maintain effectiveness for deposition on substrates with confined geometries (internal diameters down to 120 mm) and during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, without inducing deleterious oxidation or compromising adhesion.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the precise interplay between increased particle velocity and potential in-flight oxidation, and whether the optimal parameters for conventional MCrAlY deposition directly translate to HEA feedstocks in the HVAF-i7 system. Scaling to different substrate geometries may also present challenges.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled comparative study where FeCoNiCrAl HEA coatings are deposited using the HVAF-i7 torch on identical substrates under two conditions: the baseline spray distance (current setting) and an adjusted spray distance of 300 mm. Ensure all other deposition parameters remain constant.
measurements: Adhesion strength (via pull-off or scratch tests)
Oxide content (quantified by XRD or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating deposited at a 300 mm spray distance does not show a statistically significant increase in thickness (e.g., less than a 20% improvement) or if it exhibits degradation in adhesion or excessive oxidation compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

cited_evidence.kind: web:2.3. Atmospheric Plasma Spraying Coating of Samples
cited_evidence.text: Pre-heating of the processed HEA powder was carried out by placing it in the oven for 2 h at 25–150 °C, to remove any moisture present. The substrates were pre-heated with the flame of the spraying gun before the powder feed start. Plasma sprayed samples were manufactured by conventional Atmospheric Plasma Spraying system (Metco 9MC, Sulzer Metco Inc., Westbury, NY, USA) using a stand-off distance of 250 mm. Argon (Ar) gas was employed as the primary plasma operating gas and hydrogen (H2) was used as the secondary gas to escalate the whole plasma jet temperature. The feedstock ball milled powder was conveyed by a separate argon source and inoculated superficially into the spawned plasma jet at an angle of 90° concerning the anode axis. After that plasma torch assembly was mounted onto a robotic arm (YR-SK16-J00 Motoman, Yaskawa Electric Corp, Fukuoka, Japan) to navigate across the substrate holders for coating. All the parameters of the plasma spraying operation are enlisted in Table 1.

papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) spraying
papers.approach: Gas-atomized powder was sprayed with varied stand‐off distances to study in‐flight oxidation and phase transformations, thereby affecting coating hardness and microstructure.
papers.findings: An increase in spray distance led to increased alumina content (from in‐flight oxidation) and a higher fraction of the soft FCC phase—resulting in lower microhardness. This demonstrates that adjusting spray distance (and implicitly particle velocity effects) critically influences deposition efficiency and coating integrity.
papers.mechanism: High-temperature in-flight oxidation during spraying alters the phase composition; the kinetic energy (linked to particle velocity and hence spray distance) governs melt splatting and adhesion, with higher velocities promoting better deposition efficiency but also potentially enhancing oxidation if not optimized.

papers.title: Microstructure and Corrosion Behavior of Atmospheric Plasma Sprayed NiCoCrAlFe High Entropy Alloy Coating.
papers.system: NiCoCrAlFe high-entropy alloy deposited on stainless steel via atmospheric plasma spraying (APS)
papers.approach: The study used plasma spraying with appropriate pre-heating and substrate preparation to produce coatings with a lamellar, splat-based structure.
papers.findings: The coatings exhibited a homogenized microstructure with excellent adhesion and low porosity; oxidation and partial melting of particles were observed but did not significantly compromise coating quality.
papers.mechanism: Rapid heating and cooling during plasma spraying produce flattened splats with minimal oxidation; the thermal gradients and particle melting behavior control the eventual coating thickness and microstructure.

papers.title: Conventional MCrAlY Bond Coat Studies using the M3 System (Referenced in the Query)
papers.approach: Deposition experiments with the M3 system at varying particle velocities and nozzle-specific spray distances (300 mm and 350 mm) to enhance deposition efficiency.
papers.findings: A slight gain in deposition efficiency was achieved at higher particle velocities and at the identified optimal spray distances.
papers.mechanism: Higher particle velocity increases the kinetic energy of the particles, leading to improved splat flattening and adhesion, which can contribute to a thicker and more robust coating.

established: Deposition efficiency and coating microstructure in thermal spray processes depend strongly on particle velocity and spray distance.
In-flight oxidation can alter the phase composition and properties of high-entropy alloy coatings.
Optimized spray parameters (such as using optimal stand-off distances) can yield coatings with improved adhesion and reduced porosity.

approaches_tried.approach: Utilizing the M3 torch system with feedstock particles sized 15–45 μm and optimizing spray distances (300–350 mm) to improve deposition efficiency for MCrAlY bond coats.
approaches_tried.outcome: A slight increase in deposition efficiency was observed under these conditions, indicating better particle kinetics contribute to thicker coatings.

mechanisms: Higher particle velocity increases the kinetic energy of the feedstock particles, improving impact momentum, splat formation, and adhesion on the substrate.
Alterations in spray distance can modulate the in-flight oxidation and temperature exposure, thus affecting phase transformation and coating hardness.
disagreements: Some studies indicate that longer spray distances may lead to increased oxidation and a higher fraction of soft phases, reducing microhardness despite potential gains in coating build‐up.
There is a trade-off between achieving higher deposition efficiency (via increased particle velocity) and controlling oxidation levels during deposition.
open_questions: How does the HVAF-i7 torch’s particle velocity profile compare quantitatively to that of the M3 torch under similar feedstock conditions?
What is the optimal balance between increased kinetic energy (for thickness) and minimized in-flight oxidation to retain desired mechanical properties?

Can adjustments in spray distance alone overcome thickness limitations in HVAF-i7 without detrimental effects on coating integrity, especially for deposition within small internal diameters (e.g., 120 mm)?
opportunities: Investigate adjusting the HVAF-i7 deposition parameters—specifically increasing particle velocity (through optimized fuel flow and/or modified spray distance, targeting ~300–350 mm)—to overcome the inadequate thickness observed.

Explore feedstock modifications (such as slightly larger particle size distributions or enhanced alloy compositions) combined with the above parameter changes to further improve deposition efficiency.

Conduct systematic experiments to compare the deposition quality, thickness, oxidation level, and mechanical properties between baseline (15–45 μm feedstock) and modified spray conditions, particularly within constrained geometries.
Examine the interplay between particle velocity and in-flight oxidation in the HVAF-i7 system to isolate the effect of kinetic energy on coating build-up.

directions.direction: Adjust spray distance to optimize particle velocity
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the inadequate thickness by increasing particle velocity, as supported by the slight deposition efficiency gains seen in conventional MCrAlY studies at 300–350 mm (see record PMC8875499::web::007::2_3_atmospheric_plasma_spraying_coating_). This approach is straightforward to implement with existing equipment and maintains the feedstock constraints.

directions.direction: Increase fuel and oxygen flow rates to boost particle kinetic energy
directions.assessment: This intervention can enhance particle velocity but may disturb the thermal balance and affect in-flight oxidation. Although it directly increases kinetic energy, possible detriments to coating integrity must be monitored.

directions.direction: Modify the nozzle design of the HVAF-i7 torch
directions.assessment: A tailored nozzle may improve particle acceleration. However, such redesign is more complex and less immediately available than adjusting the spray distance, making it a secondary option.

While a higher feed rate could enhance overall coating thickness, it risks compromising coating quality (poorer melting, adhesion issues) and does not directly target the deposition efficiency limitation observed with the HVAF-i7 torch.

directions.direction: Pre-heat the substrate or powder to improve splat adhesion
directions.assessment: Pre-heating can improve wetting and bonding but is more supportive in nature rather than directly resolving the thickness limitation due to particle kinetic energy. It may be beneficial as a secondary measure.

choice.direction: Adjust spray distance to optimize particle velocity
choice.why: Optimizing the spray distance is directly supported by evidence in conventional MCrAlY bond coat studies and exploits the established relationship between particle velocity and deposition efficiency. This intervention can be implemented without violating feedstock or composition constraints and is expected to be effective in confined geometries (internal diameters down to 120 mm).
